books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, A. Political Parties and the Rise of the First Two-Party System

stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson, Notes on the State of Virginia, Query XIX (written 1781-82, first published in English 1787), public domain. Abridged.
stimulus.text:
“Those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God, if ever he had a chosen people, whose breasts he has made his peculiar deposit for substantial and genuine virtue. It is the focus in which he keeps alive that sacred fire, which otherwise might escape from the face of the earth.”
— Thomas Jefferson, Notes on the State of Virginia, Query XIX (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain excerpt from Jefferson's Notes on the State of Virginia (1787)
stem: In the passage, Jefferson's ideal citizen is best described as

options.text: a merchant who grows rich through foreign trade
options.misconception: Jefferson distrusted merchants and cities; his chosen people work the earth, not the counting house.

options.text: a factory worker who tends machines for wages
options.misconception: Factory wage labor is the world Hamilton's program would build, not the one Jefferson praises here.

options.text: a banker who manages the nation's money and credit
options.misconception: Bankers belong to Hamilton's commercial vision; Jefferson's passage honors the farmer, not the financier.

options.text: an independent farmer who owns and works his own land

rationales.A: Jefferson distrusted merchants and cities. His chosen people work the earth, not the counting house.
rationales.B: Factory wage labor is the world Hamilton's program would build, not the one Jefferson praises here.
rationales.C: Bankers belong to Hamilton's commercial vision. Jefferson's passage honors the farmer, not the financier.
rationales.D: Jefferson calls those who labour in the earth God's chosen people, the keepers of substantial and genuine virtue. His ideal is the yeoman farmer: self-sufficient, owning his land, and free from dependence on others. Background: only such citizens, he believed, could resist corruption and keep a republic honest.
rationales.general:
1. Read the praise. Those who labour in the earth are God's chosen people.
2. Ask who labours in the earth. The farmer, who owns his land and works it himself.
3. Ask why Jefferson honors him. The farmer's independence keeps his virtue, and the republic's, intact.
4. Put it together. The passage is a portrait of the citizen Jefferson wanted America to grow.
Remember: when a writer calls one kind of work chosen, ask whose work he is passing over.
